newsitem.title: NORWAY: Storebrand shareholders reject bank merger.
newsitem.headline: Storebrand shareholders reject bank merger.

text.p: Shareholders in Norway's largest insurance group Storebrand ASA voted on Thursday against a merger with Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse ASA, Norway's second largest bank.

Storebrand's snub to the proposal came just hours after Christiania Bank shareholders gave a green light to the plans and ends months of speculation over a power play among the company's major shareholders.
If the proposal had gone through, it would have formed Norway's largest financial group and the sixth biggest in the Nordic region.
The decision by Storebrand shareholders hung on a knife edge to the very end and lay mainly in the hands of the four largest shareholders, who each hold around a 10 percent stake.
Conglomerate Orkla voted against the proposal. The group had earlier stated concerns over the level of state ownership in the merged group.

The Norwegian state holds about 51 percent of the shares in Chrisiania Bank after it rescued the bank from a financial crisis in the late 1980s. The state would have owned about 25 percent of the merged giant.
"Our summary is that there are opportunities with the merger, but there is also uncertainty. We will vote no," Tom Vidar Rygh, Orkla's head of investments, told the shareholders' meeting.
The Norwegian state pension fund, Folketrygdfondet, and New York-based hedge fund Tiger Management had previously said they would support the merger.

Sources at the meeting said the mathematics of the vote meant that billionaire entrepreneur, Kjell Inge Roekke, who holds 10 percent with two of his privately owned companies must have turnd down the proposal.
Roekke has always declined to give his view on the deal.
